To examine something means to look at it very carefully and thoroughly so that you can understand it, find out the truth about it, or check whether something is right or wrong.

The key feeling behind the word is deliberate, focused attention. You are not just glancing at something. You are giving it your full attention, going through it carefully, and trying to learn or discover something from it.
The Different Ways It Is Used

The word "examine" works in a few different situations, and understanding each one will give you the full picture.

1. Physically Looking at Something Very Closely

When you examine a physical object or a person, you inspect it with great care, often looking for details that are not immediately obvious.

  • A doctor examines a patient — checking their body carefully, listening to their heart, looking at their eyes, to understand their health.
  • A scientist examines a sample under a microscope — looking at it closely to find information that the naked eye cannot see.
  • A jeweller examines a diamond — turning it around carefully to check its quality.
  • A detective examines the crime scene — looking at every small detail to find clues.

In all these cases, there is a clear purpose behind the looking. You are not just seeing — you are searching for something specific through careful observation.

2. Thinking About Something Carefully and Thoroughly

You can also "examine" something that is not a physical object — like an idea, an argument, a plan, a belief, or a situation. Here, examining means thinking about it deeply and seriously, turning it over in your mind, and looking at it from different angles.

  • A philosopher examines the idea of freedom — thinking about what it really means, what its limits are, and whether common assumptions about it are correct.
  • A scientist examines the evidence — going through the data carefully to see what it really shows.
  • A company examines its spending — going through all its costs in detail to understand where the money is going.
  • You might examine your own feelings or behaviour — thinking honestly and deeply about why you feel or act a certain way.

This sense carries a feeling of intellectual honesty and rigour. When you truly examine something, you do not jump to conclusions. You take your time, consider things carefully, and follow the evidence or reasoning wherever it leads.

3. Testing Someone's Knowledge or Skills (Formal Context)

In educational and official settings, "examine" means to formally test someone to see how much they know or how capable they are.

  • A university may examine students at the end of the year through written tests.
  • A medical board examines candidates before giving them a licence to practise medicine.

This is where the noun "examination" (often shortened to "exam") comes from — it is the formal test itself. The person conducting the test is called an examiner.

4. Questioning Someone in a Formal or Legal Setting

In law, "examine" means to formally question a witness or a person in order to get information or test the truth of what they are saying.

  • A lawyer examines a witness in court — asking them a series of careful questions to reveal the truth or to challenge their version of events.

This sense is closely related to the general idea of the word — you are trying to get to the truth through careful, deliberate questioning.

No matter which context you see "examine" in, the same core idea is always present:

Careful, thorough, purposeful attention — aimed at understanding, discovering, or verifying the truth.

It is never a casual or lazy act. Examining something always takes effort, focus, and intent.

Because you are a learner, it helps to understand how "examine" is different from words that seem similar.

Look at is neutral and casual. You can "look at" something without any real purpose or depth.

Inspect is close in meaning to "examine," but "inspect" usually focuses on checking for faults, correctness, or compliance — like a safety inspector inspecting a building. "Examine" is slightly broader and also includes studying for understanding, not just checking for problems.

Study means spending a long period of time learning about something. You study a subject over weeks or months. "Examine" suggests a more focused, intensive act that happens at a specific moment.

Investigate focuses specifically on uncovering something hidden or unknown, often a problem or a mystery. "Examine" can be part of an investigation, but it does not always imply a mystery or wrongdoing.

Scrutinise is very close to "examine" but is even more intense — it suggests looking at every tiny detail with almost suspicious thoroughness.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Examine" is a slightly formal word. It is perfectly natural in everyday speech, but it carries more weight and seriousness than casual words like "look at" or "check." When you use it, you are signalling that the attention being given is serious, careful, and purposeful. This is why it appears frequently in academic writing, medical contexts, legal settings, and thoughtful conversation.
Key Forms of the Word You Will Encounter

• Examine — the base verb ("Please examine this document.")
  • Examined — past tense ("The doctor examined the patient.")
  • Examining — present participle ("She is still examining the evidence.")
  • Examination — the noun form, meaning the act of examining, or a formal test ("The examination revealed a fracture." / "I passed my final examination.")
  • Examiner — a person who examines someone, especially in a formal or testing context ("The examiner asked me three difficult questions.")
  • Examinee — the person being examined or tested ("Each examinee had three hours to complete the paper.")

If someone asks you to explain "examine" simply, you could say:

"To examine something means to look at it, think about it, or go through it very carefully — because you want to understand it, find the truth, or check something."

But now you know far more than that simple sentence. You know that this one word travels across physical inspection, deep intellectual thought, formal testing, and legal questioning — and in every case, it carries the same spirit: deliberate, careful, thorough attention in the pursuit of understanding or truth.
